summary: International education this week has three main threads. First, China has formally put "running schools abroad" on the agenda: on 29 October the China Annual Conference for International Education held its first special forum on overseas campuses; a representative of the Ministry of Education's Department of International Cooperation and Exchange advocated a "small but excellent, people-centred, asset-light" model, said the Guidelines for Higher Education Institutions Running Schools Abroad were being revised, and that an annual reporting system for overseas campuses was being explored. Second, Switzerland's return to Erasmus+ gained another vote: the National Council's Committee for Science, Education and Culture (WBK-N) on 22–23 October recommended approval of 2027 funding by 17 votes to 8, with a plenary vote expected in December; in the same week, the EuroTech Universities Alliance, of which EPFL is a member, held a summit in Brussels on 28 October on turning frontier technology into European competitiveness and technological sovereignty. Third, quantum and AI education are becoming more institutional: Singapore Management University signed with quantum-computing company QpiAI on 27 October, giving faculty and students access to the 64-qubit Kaveri quantum computer; India has confirmed construction of its first "quantum and AI university campus" in Amaravati, with 7.307 billion rupees over five years. At the same time, public comment on the US OPT-fee proposal closes on 9 November, New Zealand tightened student visas from 27 October, and English-speaking countries' attractiveness to international students remains under pressure; US university gifts continue to flow toward hands-on training space and talent development.
trends: "Asset-light" has become a consensus in transnational education: China's Ministry of Education explicitly advocates "small but excellent, people-centred, asset-light"; Hebei University of Technology's Finland campus and Northwest A&F University's Tashkent campus both rely on local university resources, consistent with last week's path of an SMU centre in Shenzhen and HKU Business School's plan to start with joint training in Hanoi.

Academic integration between Switzerland and Europe continues: both key National Council committees have supported Erasmus+ funding, and the December plenary vote is the critical point; Europe's leading technical universities are lobbying as an alliance for the 2028–2034 EU budget.

Quantum education is shifting from "teaching principles" to "using real machines and issuing certificates": SMU is obtaining quantum compute through a company partnership and including professional certification, and 80% of those to be trained at India's new quantum and AI campus will come from skills-certification programmes.

English-speaking countries continue to tighten policy on international students (the US OPT-fee proposal, limits on work rights in New Zealand). The diversion of international students toward Europe and Asia is worth continued tracking.

No verified major new higher-education developments in the Middle East were found in this time window. THE World University Rankings 2027 (released 30 September) and the OECD Education at a Glance 2026 (released 29 September) fall outside this edition's window and are not repeated here.
footer: All facts and figures in this brief are taken from the public sources listed; the original texts prevail. Time window: 2026-10-23 to 2026-10-30 (Zurich time); the Gies matching gift (20 October) is included as background. This edition has no peer-reviewed papers, newly released annual reports this week, or Nature/Science-level results, and no permanent record was created.

items.title: China Annual Conference for International Education holds its first special forum on overseas campuses: the Ministry of Education advocates "small but excellent, asset-light" and is revising the guidelines
items.what: According to a 29 October notice from Hebei University of Technology, the 2026 China Annual Conference for International Education (hosted by the China Education Association for International Exchange, theme "Openness breeds the new, cooperation goes far") held a forum that day at the China National Convention Center in Beijing on "exploring paths and practical development of running schools abroad", the first special forum on the subject since the conference began. Xi Ru, a second-level inspector at the Ministry of Education's Department of International Cooperation and Exchange, said in a keynote that China's running of schools abroad is still at an early stage of development; the next steps will be to insist on safety, quality and practical results, optimise the regional and country layout, improve risk-prevention mechanisms, accelerate revision of relevant policy documents, explore an annual reporting system and a monitoring-indicator system, and advocate a "small but excellent, people-centred, asset-light" model. Cases include Hebei University of Technology's Finland campus (relying on resources of Finland's LUT University, China's first undergraduate-level overseas campus in a developed European or American country), Northwest A&F University's Tashkent campus, and Beijing Language and Culture University's Kazakhstan campus.
items.why: This is the first time Chinese officialdom has concentrated discussion of "going out" to run schools at the highest-level annual conference on international education, and it has set a clear policy direction: asset-light, quality-first, and annual reporting. The Finland campus model of relying on a local university's resources and exporting curriculum and faculty shows that Chinese universities already have a replicable precedent for operating in Europe.
items.src: Hebei University of Technology news site

items.title: Switzerland's return to Erasmus+ gains another vote: the National Council education committee recommends approval of 2027 funding by 17 votes to 8
items.what: According to the Swiss Federation for Adult Learning (SVEB / alice.ch) on 23 October, the National Council's Committee for Science, Education and Culture (WBK-N), at its meeting of 22–23 October, recommended by 17 votes to 8 that the National Council consider and support the committed appropriation for Switzerland to take part in Erasmus+ in 2027. The Council of States had already approved the 192.6 million Swiss franc appropriation on 1 October by 23 votes to 19, with 2 abstentions, and the National Council Finance Committee supported it on 16 October by 18 votes to 7. The National Council's final plenary vote is expected in the December winter session. According to federal parliamentary reporting, 2027 is the last year of the current Erasmus+ programme, and participation from 2028 will require a separate proposal from the Federal Council.
items.why: Both key National Council committees (finance and education) have now given clear support, further raising the likelihood of approval at the December plenary. Once approved, students and faculty at Swiss institutions will receive European mobility and cooperation funding on equal terms with EU member states.
items.src: SVEB / alice.ch; Swiss Federal Assembly news (1 October)

items.title: EuroTech Universities Alliance summit in Brussels: EPFL, TUM, DTU and three other members focus on frontier technology and European technological sovereignty
items.what: According to a 27 October notice from Institut Polytechnique de Paris (IP Paris), the EuroTech Universities Alliance held its 2026 summit in Brussels on 28 October, themed "Unlocking Frontier Tech for Europe", chaired by alliance president Thierry Coulhon, president of IP Paris. Expected guests included European Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen, responsible for technological sovereignty, security and democracy, and Bernard Magenhann, director-general of the Joint Research Centre. Discussion focused on four areas — digital and enabling technologies, clean technology and energy, health and biotechnology, and security and space — and on how to take laboratory results to market. The summit also marked the alliance's 15th anniversary. Members are the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), IP Paris, Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e) and the Technical University of Munich (TUM), and a "Strategy 2030" has been adopted.
items.why: The EU is setting its next research and innovation priorities and the 2028–2034 budget. Leading technical universities are speaking collectively as an alliance to get "translation of frontier technology" into the policy and funding framework. Earlier this month, 271 European universities also signed a statement calling for explicit support for university alliances in the 2028–2034 budget.

items.title: Singapore Management University signs a quantum-AI memorandum with QpiAI: faculty and students will have access to a 64-qubit quantum computer
items.what: According to a 27 October notice from Singapore Management University's School of Computing and Information Systems, Indian full-stack quantum-computing company QpiAI signed a two-year memorandum of understanding with SMU, also QpiAI's first step into Singapore. SMU becomes the first higher-education institution in Singapore to partner with QpiAI, and researchers and students will have access to QpiAI's 64-qubit Kaveri quantum computer and the QCloud platform. The cooperation covers four areas: finance and industrial applications (fintech, smart cities, supply chains); frontier quantum-AI research (quantum algorithms, quantum machine learning, post-quantum cryptography); talent development (joint training, professional certification, hands-on practice, themed workshops); and an innovation ecosystem (start-up support and participation in national and international quantum programmes).
items.why: Quantum education is shifting from "teaching principles" to "using real machines": a university known for business and finance is obtaining quantum compute directly through a company partnership and including professional certification in the cooperation. This shows that non-STEM universities are also entering quantum education quickly through industry partnerships.
items.src: SMU School of Computing and Information Systems

items.title: India confirms construction of its first "quantum and AI university campus" in Amaravati: 7.307 billion rupees over five years
items.what: According to The Hindu BusinessLine on 26 October, the Government of Andhra Pradesh is working with the National Institute of Electronics and Information Technology (NIELIT) to build India's first specialised "quantum and AI university campus" in Amaravati, on 8.5 acres, with planned spending of 7.307 billion rupees over five years, all from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. The campus will sit under NIELIT's existing "deemed university" framework and will offer undergraduate, master's, doctoral, diploma and executive programmes in quantum computing, artificial intelligence and machine learning, data science, chip design, VLSI and high-performance computing. It plans to train about 8,250 people over five years, 1,650 through degree programmes and 6,600 through skills and certification programmes. The report notes that Nvidia, which had earlier been announced as a partner, is currently involved only in a parallel "AI Living Lab", not in the university itself.
items.why: This is a university campus newly built with an overall "quantum + AI" positioning, fully funded by government, and with non-degree skills certification accounting for 80% of those trained. It shows that countries are treating quantum talent development as national industrial policy, and that short-term certification is larger in scale than full degrees.

items.title: English-speaking countries' attractiveness for study abroad is under pressure: public comment on the US OPT-fee proposal closes on 9 November; New Zealand tightens student visas from 27 October
items.what: According to CNA on 27 October, US education groups have warned that a Trump administration proposal to charge universities $70,000 for each international student's OPT (practical-training) recommendation and $30,000 for each renewal could push foreign students to other countries. The proposal is not yet in effect; the public-comment period ends on 9 November, and a final rule would take effect 60 days after publication (as explained by the University of California, Irvine international centre). The Minnesota Reformer reported on 28 October that more than half of US universities saw a drop in international-student applications in 2025–26, and that fall 2026 enrolment at St. Cloud State University had fallen, about half of it due to international-student visa issues. According to Immigration New Zealand, from 27 October new research master's students will no longer have unlimited work rights while studying, but a uniform 25 hours a week; English proficiency is explicitly a key factor in visa assessment; at the same time, student visas will remain valid for two months after a course ends, rather than one.
items.why: US pathways for internships and post-graduation work are becoming expensive and uncertain, and countries such as New Zealand and Australia are also tightening. The flow of international students and early-career scholars is being reorganised, and the relative attractiveness of Europe (including Switzerland) and Asia is rising.
items.src: CNA; Minnesota Reformer; UCI International Center; Immigration New Zealand

items.title: Gifts flow toward "hands-on training + talent development": Caltech and JPL receive $27.5 million; the University of Illinois receives a $100 million matching-gift pledge
items.what: On 28 October, the California Institute of Technology announced that philanthropists Foster and Coco Stanback had given a total of $27.5 million to Caltech and to the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), which Caltech manages for NASA: $20 million to build a New Space Makerspace at JPL and to fund Caltech-led education and talent programmes (including a makerspace fellows programme for community-college students, interns and postdocs); and $7.5 million to renovate and expand hypersonics research facilities. The same day, Villanova University announced a $25 million gift from alumni Justin and Victoria Gmelich, counted toward its $1.25 billion comprehensive campaign. Slightly earlier, on 20 October, the University of Illinois announced that alumnus Larry Gies had pledged a $100 million matching gift to the Gies College of Business, which held a celebration on 25 October.
items.why: Gifts to US universities are increasingly directed at spaces where students can work with their hands, and at talent development for a wider group of students (including community-college students). Matching gifts remain a core tool for amplifying donations.
items.src: Caltech News; Villanova University; Gies College of Business
